introduction.heading: What is a Payment System?
introduction.description: Adding payments to a web app almost always means integrating a payment processor (Stripe, PayPal, Braintree...) rather than handling card numbers yourself - actually storing or transmitting raw card data puts you in a heavy compliance regime (PCI-DSS) that isn't worth it for the vast majority of apps. The shape is the same everywhere: the browser collects card details directly into the processor's own SDK (never your server), your backend creates a charge for a specific amount, and a server-to-server webhook - not the browser's "it worked!" - is what actually confirms the money moved. Everything below uses Stripe's terms since it's the most common, but the concepts (tokenization, webhooks, idempotency) map directly onto any processor.

concepts.title: Tokenization
concepts.description: Card details are collected by the processor's own SDK and exchanged for a token before your code ever sees them - your server only ever handles the token

concepts.title: Payment Intents
concepts.description: The object that tracks one payment through its full lifecycle - created, needs confirmation, may need extra authentication, then succeeds or fails

concepts.title: Webhooks
concepts.description: Signed, server-to-server events that are the real source of truth - the client reporting success is not confirmation that you got paid

concepts.title: Idempotency Keys
concepts.description: A unique key attached to a charge request so retrying it after a timeout or double-click can't create a second charge

concepts.title: Refunds vs Disputes
concepts.description: A refund is something you initiate and control; a dispute (chargeback) is initiated by the customer's bank and has its own evidence deadline

flow.heading: The Payment Flow
flow.description: Every card payment follows the same shape regardless of processor: the browser collects card details without your server ever seeing them, your server creates a charge for a known amount, and a webhook confirms what actually happened. Where the two common integration strategies differ is who builds the payment form - a hosted checkout page redirects the user to the processor entirely, while embedded elements keep the user on your page but still hand card input directly to the processor's SDK.

gettingStarted.heading: Getting Started
steps: Install the processor's server SDK (npm install stripe) and load its client-side SDK/script for collecting card details
Keep the secret key server-side only - only the publishable key is ever safe to ship to the browser
Create a PaymentIntent or Checkout Session on your server for the exact amount, in the smallest currency unit (cents)
Collect card details with the processor's hosted fields/Elements or redirect to its hosted checkout - your server never sees the card number
Treat the client's reported success as provisional - only update your database once a webhook confirms the payment server-side
Verify every webhook's signature against your webhook signing secret before trusting anything in its payload
Attach an idempotency key to charge-creating requests so a retried request after a network blip can't double-charge
Handle refunds and disputes as separate flows from the original charge - a refund is you-initiated, a dispute is bank-initiated

fullExample.heading: Full Example, Step by Step
fullExample.title: Create a charge, verify the webhook, and issue a refund
fullExample.description: This example wires together creating a PaymentIntent, confirming payment via a webhook, and refunding an order into one small Express file. Click through the steps to see which lines each one is talking about.

steps.label: Create the charge with an idempotency key
steps.explanation: The amount comes from the order looked up on the server (never trust an amount sent from the client) and the idempotency key is derived from the order id - retrying this exact request, say after a timeout, reuses the same PaymentIntent instead of creating a second one.

steps.label: Webhooks need the raw body, not parsed JSON
steps.explanation: Signature verification hashes the exact bytes Stripe sent - if any body-parsing middleware runs first and reserializes the JSON, the signature check fails even for a legitimate event, so this route uses express.raw() instead of express.json().

steps.label: Verify the signature before trusting anything
steps.explanation: constructEvent() recomputes the expected signature from the raw body and your webhook signing secret - if it doesn't match, the request didn't really come from Stripe, or the payload was altered in transit, so it's rejected outright.

steps.label: The webhook confirms payment, not the browser
steps.explanation: Only after this event arrives does the order get marked "paid" - a client-side redirect to a success page just means the browser thinks it worked, and a dropped connection or closed tab shouldn't be able to leave an order permanently marked paid when it wasn't.

steps.label: Refunding is a separate flow
steps.explanation: A refund reverses money on an existing PaymentIntent - it doesn't touch idempotency keys or webhooks for the original charge, and Stripe fires its own charge.refunded webhook that a real app would also listen for.
